stances.claim: Hard work alone is insufficient to solve the backlog -- novel methods like arbitration/mediation and plea bargaining are needed to reduce both the stock and the flow of cases.
Courts should make more aggressive use of judgment on pleadings and summary judgments to make short shrift of patently unmeritorious cases.
The SC itself prolongs cases by requesting comments on unmeritorious petitions; it should dismiss or deny outright cases that are clearly bereft of merit.
More than 80% of full decisions merely affirm or reiterate settled jurisprudence -- extensive resort to minute resolutions and unsigned decisions would greatly help.
The full digitization of the judiciary -- from filing to live proceedings to judgment service -- is long overdue and should be hastened and made comprehensive.
J. Reyes's CA backlog reduction model is proven -- the SC should use his expertise and experience without reinventing the wheel.

notable_anecdotes: The SC's 'more than 80 percent' heuristic: if that many decisions merely affirm or reiterate settled jurisprudence, the Court is consuming enormous ponencia resources for cases that could be disposed of in minutes via minute resolutions.
E-courts started but limited -- current websites show only decisions and resolutions, not the progression of cases from stage to stage; parties and lawyers cannot track exact case status online.
J. Andres B. Reyes Jr.'s achievement in trimming the CA backlog -- cited as the model to import to the SC -- 'the wheel need not be reinvented.'
The 'overdue process' coinage: parties invoking due-process requirements not to ensure fairness but to gain unfair advantage or delay judgment.

decision_framework_signals: Reduce case stock via arbitration/mediation in civil/commercial and plea bargaining in criminal cases
Reduce case flow via aggressive use of summary judgment and judgment on the pleadings
Apply the SC's own motu proprio dismissal power to clearly unmeritorious petitions -- stop requiring comments

Publish periodic case-progress reports on the SC website as a transparency and accountability tool

Import proven models (Reyes CA method) rather than designing new systems from scratch
one_paragraph_summary: Following up the December 24 column on judicial qualities, Panganiban addresses the systemic side of docket unclogging. Given 980,000 pending cases across 2,400 trial courts, hard work alone is insufficient -- the following should be encouraged: arbitration and mediation (especially in commercial and civil cases) and plea bargaining in criminal cases. On the inflow side, courts must curtail litigants who invoke 'overdue process' for unfair advantage, making more aggressive use of the Rules of Court's underused shortcuts -- judgment on the pleadings and summary judgments. He turns the lens on the SC itself: it prolongs cases by requesting comments on clearly unmeritorious petitions rather than dismissing them outright, and since more than 80% of full decisions merely affirm lower courts or reiterate settled jurisprudence, the Court should resort far more extensively to minute resolutions and unsigned decisions. He also proposes periodic progress reports on the SC website for transparency. The most transformational prescription is full E-court digitization -- long overdue since he began his judicial career -- from the preparation and filing of pleadings through live proceedings to the service of judgments, for all courts from the SC to the lowest trial courts; current websites show only decisions and resolutions, not case progression. He closes by recommending the SC import J. Andres B. Reyes Jr.'s proven CA backlog-reduction model: 'the wheel need not be reinvented.'
